topics.title: Spelling: -dge, -ge, kn, gn, wr
topics.intro: These words follow a pattern. Learn the pattern, and you can spell hundreds of words!
topics.teach: Pick one pattern and give two more words that follow it.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find a word with today’s pattern in a book or on a sign.

topics.intro: These words follow a pattern. Learn the pattern, and you can spell hundreds of words!

topics.talk: Ask {him} to find a word with today’s pattern in a book or on a sign.

topics.title: Beginnings: un-, dis-, re-
topics.intro: A prefix goes at the start of a word and changes its meaning. un- and dis- mean “not”; re- means “again”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for the opposite of “lock”, “like” and “tidy” using a prefix.

topics.title: One and many: plurals
topics.intro: Most words add -s for more than one. Words ending s, x, sh or ch add -es. Some words change completely: one mouse, two mice!
topics.teach: Explain how to make “baby” and “box” plural.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for the plural of “tooth”, “foot” and “child”.

topics.title: Compound words
topics.intro: A compound word is two words joined together: foot + ball = football, sun + flower = sunflower.
topics.teach: Explain what a compound word is, with two examples.
topics.talk: Race to find compound words around the house (toothbrush, cupboard…).

topics.title: Better sentences
topics.intro: Great writers make sentences better: add adjectives to nouns, use adverbs to say how, and join ideas with and, but, because, when and if.
topics.teach: Make this sentence better: “The car went.”
topics.talk: Say a dull sentence and ask {him} to make it exciting.

topics.title: Speech marks
topics.intro: Inverted commas (speech marks) go around the words someone actually says: “Ready for launch!” said the captain.
topics.teach: Explain where the speech marks go in a sentence.
topics.talk: Write a comic strip together and turn the speech bubbles into sentences with speech marks.

items.sentence: The knight wore a ___ on his tunic.
items.clue: a little sign you pin on
items.explain: After a short vowel, the “j” sound is -dge: badge, bridge, hedge.
items.learn: **badge**: After a short vowel, the “j” sound is -dge: badge, bridge, hedge.

items.sentence: A ___ dragon landed on the castle.
items.explain: After a long vowel, just -ge: huge, page, cage.
items.learn: **huge**: After a long vowel, just -ge: huge, page, cage.

items.sentence: I would like a ___ ice cream, please.
___ on the door before you go in.

items.explain: Silent k, and -ow at the end.
items.learn: **know**: Silent k, and -ow at the end.

items.sentence: The dog likes to ___ on a bone.
He wears a watch on his ___.

items.explain: -le is the most common ending: lit-tle, with double t.
items.learn: **little**: -le is the most common ending: lit-tle, with double t.

items.sentence: Stand in the ___ of the line.
The train went into a dark ___.
items.explain: Some words end -el: tunnel, camel, travel.
items.learn: **tunnel**: Some words end -el: tunnel, camel, travel.

items.sentence: I would like to ___ to the Moon.

items.clue: iron, steel or gold, for example
items.explain: Some words end -al: metal, pedal, animal.
items.learn: **metal**: Some words end -al: metal, pedal, animal.

items.sentence: Push the ___ to make the bike go.
items.clue: you push it with your foot
where poorly people are cared for

items.explain: Some words end -il: pencil, fossil, nostril.
items.learn: **pencil**: Some words end -il: pencil, fossil, nostril.

items.explain: After w, a says “o”: want, watch, wash.
items.learn: **want**: After w, a says “o”: want, watch, wash.

items.explain: w-a-t-c-h: a says “o”, and -tch after a short vowel.
items.learn: **watch**: w-a-t-c-h: a says “o”, and -tch after a short vowel.

items.clue: a group of letters that means something
items.explain: After w, or says “ur”: word, work, world.
items.learn: **word**: After w, or says “ur”: word, work, world.

items.explain: After w, ar says “or”: war, warm.
items.learn: **warm**: After w, ar says “or”: war, warm.

items.explain: o says “u” as in cup: o-ther.
items.learn: **other**: o says “u” as in cup: o-ther.

items.clue: the first day of the school week
items.explain: Capital M, and o says “u”: Mon-day.
items.learn: **Monday**: Capital M, and o says “u”: Mon-day.

items.sentence: Turn the ___ to start the engine.

items.clue: a cheeky animal with a tail
items.explain: o says “u” AND ey says “ee”: mon-key.
items.learn: **monkey**: o says “u” AND ey says “ee”: mon-key.

items.explain: un- means not: unhappy = not happy.

items.prompt: Which word means the opposite of “lock”?

items.explain: dis + appear: one s, double p (because appear has a double p).

options.feedback: “under” is a whole word: there is no “der” on its own.
“uncle” is a whole word, not un + cle.

items.explain: unkind = un + kind. A prefix is added to a word that makes sense on its own.
Consonant + y: change y to i and add -es.
Some plurals change completely: mouse → mice.
foot → feet, tooth → teeth, goose → geese.
Some words stay the same: one sheep, ten sheep. Fish and deer too!

options.feedback: Both parts must be real words.
Look for two whole words.

items.explain: Join them with no gap: sunflower.

options.feedback: play + ing: -ing is an ending, not a word.
-er is an ending, not a word.

items.prompt: Which word joins with “fire” to make a compound word?

options.feedback: -ing is an ending, not a word.
-ed is an ending.

items.explain: fire + work = firework. Also fireman, fireplace, firefly!

items.prompt: Which sentence has the best expanded noun phrase?

options.text: The gleaming red racing car zoomed past.
The car zoomed past us very, very quickly.
options.feedback: That adds an adverb (how it zoomed), but the noun “car” has no describing words.

options.text: Yesterday, after lunch, the car zoomed past.
options.feedback: That tells us when, but the noun “car” has no describing words.

items.explain: “the gleaming red racing car” gives the reader a clear picture.

items.prompt: Which adverb best fits? “The spy crept ___ past the guard.”

options.feedback: A spy creeping past a guard wants to be quiet!
It doesn’t tell us how a spy sneaks.

items.explain: Adverbs tell us how: crept silently.

items.prompt: Which joining word gives a CHOICE?

options.feedback: “and” adds another idea.
“but” shows a contrast.

items.prompt: Choose the best joining word: “I hope ___ we win the race.”

options.feedback: “I hope or we win” doesn’t make sense.
“I hope but we win” doesn’t make sense.

items.explain: “that” introduces what you hope: I hope that we win.

items.prompt: What kind of sentence is this? “Mars is the red planet.”

options.feedback: It doesn’t ask anything.
It doesn’t tell anyone to do something.
It is a calm fact, with a full stop.

items.explain: A statement tells you something and ends with a full stop.

items.prompt: Which sentence is in the PAST tense all the way through?

options.text: The knight rode to the castle and knocked on the door.
The knight rode to the castle and knocks on the door.
options.feedback: “knocks” is present tense. Keep the tense the same.

options.text: The knight rides to the castle and knocked on the door.
options.feedback: “rides” is present. Both verbs should be past.

items.explain: Keep the tense the same: rode… knocked.

options.feedback: With “we”, use “were”.
With “we”, use “are” (now) or “were” (past).

items.explain: I was, you were, he was, we were, they were.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows something that WAS happening for a while?

options.text: The rain was falling all night.
The rain falls every single night.
options.feedback: That is present tense.

options.text: The rain will fall all night long.
options.feedback: That is future.

items.explain: “was falling” is the past progressive: it was going on for a while.

items.prompt: Which sentence has the speech marks in the right place?

options.feedback: Only the words that are SPOKEN go inside.
The captain didn’t say “shouted the captain”!

items.explain: Speech marks go round the exact words spoken.

items.prompt: In “I can fly!” said the hero, which words were spoken?

options.feedback: Those words tell us WHO spoke.
That is who said it.

items.explain: The words inside the speech marks are the ones spoken aloud.

options.feedback: You need a comma (or ! or ?) before the closing speech marks.
Use a comma, not a full stop, when “said Rosa” follows.

items.explain: When the sentence carries on after the speech, put a comma before the closing speech marks.

options.feedback: Spoken words start with a capital letter.
Put a comma before the speech, and the full stop inside.

items.explain: Comma before the speech, capital letter to start it, punctuation inside the closing marks.

items.prompt: Which is the most exciting word to use instead of “said”? “Help!” ___ the princess.

options.feedback: “said” is fine, but “screamed” tells us how she said it.
“told” doesn’t fit here.

items.explain: Words like screamed, whispered and bellowed show HOW someone spoke.

sentences.title: Speech marks
sentences.prompt: Write what a racing driver says at the start of a race. Use speech marks and “said”.

checks.msg: Put speech marks around the spoken words: “…”
Use the word “said” (or try “shouted”, but keep “said” this time).

sentences.tip: Only the spoken words go inside the speech marks.

sentences.title: Use “if”
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence using “if”: “If I were a superhero, I would…”

checks.msg: Finish the idea: what would you do?

sentences.model: If I were a superhero, I would fly to the Moon.
sentences.tip: “if” sets up something that might happen.

sentences.title: Add an adverb
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence about a spy using an adverb ending in -ly, like “silently” or “quickly”.
sentences.model: The spy crept silently past the guard.
sentences.tip: Adverbs tell the reader HOW something happened.

sentences.title: A command
sentences.prompt: Write a command for a robot. Start with a bossy verb like “Go”, “Stop” or “Pick”.

checks.msg: Start with a bossy verb, like Go, Stop or Pick.

sentences.tip: Commands start with a verb that tells someone what to do.

sentences.title: A super noun phrase
sentences.prompt: Describe a dinosaur using “The” plus TWO adjectives before the noun, like “The huge, scaly dinosaur…”.

checks.msg: Start with “The” and two describing words.
Finish your sentence: what did the dinosaur do?

sentences.model: The huge, scaly dinosaur stomped through the jungle.
sentences.tip: Two adjectives can be separated by a comma: the huge, scaly dinosaur.

sentences.title: Two joining words
sentences.prompt: Write ONE sentence about a castle that uses both “and” and “but”.
sentences.model: The castle was big and strong, but the dragon was stronger.
sentences.tip: “and” adds an idea; “but” adds a surprise.
